interactions.title: Kenzo recounts initiation and Bhishma’s message about Shakun’s stolen heart
lines: Seeker: Well, I can tell you I am not a Mystai of Bhishma, and also I'm not dead. So both of those things are true.

Kenzo: Kenzo kind of like staggers, you know, so I'm assuming it's like the cafeteria, so there's like table and chairs—and Kenzo kind of, kind of staggers over and sits down and it's just like, like kind of one hand's like you know, on his staff, just kind of leaning up against it, and the other just you know barely kind of keeping his head above the table. I kind of looks at everybody. I really need to stop having these brushes with death. I feel like I learned a lot when I get into that portal, but it's not—it's not a good for my health, I don't think.
Seeker: Dying generally is not considered good for your health, yeah.
Kenzo: I think that might be the definition there I'm missing. Seeker, thank you for, for, for at least giving me a little bit of life force back, but—

Seeker: You had me worried there for, for a second. I'd love to hear again more about what you saw and experienced. I also saw and experienced some very interesting things, but I think it was quite different for you.
Kenzo: Well, you didn't accept the offer, did you? Know—
Seeker: I came just to the edge.
Kenzo: We—Seeker, I wanted to see what you saw. I'm curious what you saw.
Seeker: Well, you know, I've got a lot of ideas now. It's this amazing kind of multi, multi sensory performance, kind of historical immersive experience.

Seeker: And more specifically, I'm thinking that perhaps when we return from this adventure, we could create something like it and charge admission. But what we, we think that we experienced what the young disciples here in this monastery would have experienced as part of an initiation ritual that takes you, in a first-person way, through the story of Bhishma herself, from her perspective. That was, as far as I could tell, what was happening. Do you think so, Kenzo?
Seeker: So crucial moment arrived after the journey leading the people into Dunmar. Of—everybody's like dying and starving, and then we're all gonna die, and then—what happened?
Kenzo: Well, the critical moment was when we were asked if we would give our lives for Jeevali. At least I was asked if I'd give my life for her.

Seeker: Yeah, will you give your life for Jeevali? And I thought, well, that's very interesting. I could see how young monks who've been studying the story of Bhishma and Jeevali their whole lives up to this point, and are now pledging their devotion, perhaps would agree to give their lives in some metaphorical sense and not literally die at that moment for Jeevali. But I thought not to take the chance myself at that moment. Kenzo, on the other hand, seems to have gone for it. I died, yeah, I—
Seeker: I didn't panic exactly, but it was—
Kenzo: I died there. This is now, I think, the third time I've done—wait, hold on, this—this is the third time that Kenzo's hit zero.
DM: However, you've never actually died before.
Kenzo: No. Oh yeah, yeah but, but I've had, I've had to do death saving throws.

Seeker: So up to this point we've been like seeing the beautiful plains of the story of the settling of the, the you know the ride into Dunmar—and the fertile ground turn into ash and—and, and the river, and the moments of decision, and Jeevali's tears flowing. But then after that, it was all just sandstone for me.

Kenzo: Yeah, on—its—and Seeker, Seeker speaks the truth: I am now a Mystai of Bhishma. I completed the initiation ritual. This is, I think, exactly what generations of Mystai before me have also experienced.

Kenzo: Of course, as a, as a Lakan Mystai, this family of god's is his kin to me, so it wasn't a hard choice to make in this moment for me. And given my heritage and my connection to the gods here, it was, it was an easy decision to make. And I do have, I think, some clarity—or perhaps more mystery—but a bit more of an understanding, I think, of maybe what is happening amongst the gods. When I, when I—when I awoke, the pond area at the center of the, of the, of the center of the pentagon was alive with vibrancy. It was, it was, it was bursting with birds and, and life, the water so crystal and beautiful, and I saw—
Seeker: Trip, Perhaps I was the one experiencing the illusion.

Kenzo: What is reality but a relative set of—I think that's an important question, actually, the nature of reality. But what I saw, though was, was a small, small group of crystal butterflies emerging from the spray of the fountain, and it took on the shape of some words that said, she is with me, as always, but cannot reach Karawa.
Seeker: Oh, I remember you asking a question. You were talking, I think. I did—praying.
Kenzo: I asked, I asked where she was. [garbled]. And responded that she was with me.
Delwath: Does it—remind me, Bhishma is Shakun's father or mother?
Seeker: Mother, mother. Yeah, nope, okay.
Delwath: And she's the actual god?
Kenzo: Yeah, this is the demigod.
Delwath: Which one was the five siblings?
DM: Laka, Jeevali, Aagir, Chidya and Sonkar. Laka is Shakun's father.
Seeker: Okay, and Bhishma starts as a human.
DM: Bhishma starts as a human but becomes a demigod, as does Shakun.
Kenzo: Oh, she starts as human, see.
Delwath: Born to Laka and Bhishma, right? So starts as, as [garbled].
Kenzo: And Kenzo is a Lakan Mystai, so before all of this was, was a—was within Mystai, but—
Delwath: You just need to become a Shakun Mystai and collect the whole family set.

Kenzo: That's the, the fucking journey now. I mean, I guess that's probably going to happen, unless we go back to figure out what the hell's going on in Karawa. But any case, Bhishma responded that law that Shakun is with me, as always, but cannot reach Karawa. Something has been taken that should be there, something that helps her reach the world. Find it and bring it back. And part of what I saw as I, as I heard these words from the crystal, crystal set of butterflies was an image of a beating heart made of stone.
Kenzo: And what did the stone look like?
Kenzo: Reddish, it—okay. I'm—reddish ochre stone.
Seeker: Men—a shaped stone or a rough one? Reddish rough ochre stone, like—I mean that describes this the sandstone that the Mesa of where the temple of Shakun is carved.

Kenzo: But I, you know, it—is it a literal answer, to return this, this stone somehow to, to Karawa? Perhaps. Where this stone is, I have no sense but, but I was able to commune with Bhishma. I was able to communicate with Bhishma. And I think our instincts are right that there is an object that we have to find. And I don't think that this particular part, at least, relates to—or it doesn't seem, at least, to relate to—these fragments of jade. This stone seems to be to be something different. So yet another lost object that needs to be recovered. And who knows, maybe also connected to this, the set of mysteries of these, these objects being hoarded by the open—the Open Society, the Open Scroll, by maybe Agata Dust Mother. I don't know.
Kenzo: Crossing over to the world beyond, beyond is not something I want to do more of. But I have a feeling is not going to be the last one for myself, or maybe all of us that a lot of experience.
Seeker: I wonder if there's any specific meaning to the heart, in particular, of Shakun, or if it is her heart or someone else's. Or is their heart imagery anywhere in the stories, Tim?
Seeker: Of Shakun or the associated Dunmari pantheon.
Kenzo: Who doesn't know that to you?
DM: Yeah, so not really. So I guess—actually, Seeker, why don't you roll Religion? Kenzo, I think you would, you would know—in the stories, you know, it's, um—

DM: Has studied. Well, um, I mean there's, there's not a lot of, of sort of heart imagery. The closest, maybe, is there sort of imagery of—there's like you know there's, there's like stories of places that are connected to the gods and like things that are sacred, right? So like I mean obviously like this monastery right, is—you know this kind of thing comes up a lot right is, is a place that somehow has a particular connection to a god, or, or sometimes the thing that has a particular connection to a god. But, um, but heart specifically? No, there's nothing that, that, that you can sort of—that you can think of, specifically about Shakun or Laka or any of that sort of family.

DM: Seeker, you have—so there's not a lot of books on Dunmari pantheon specifically that you've studied back in the dwarven archives, or even the time you spent coming through Chardon. I'm—the thing that comes to your mind that maybe is connected is definitely the idea that god's can, you know—sort of by analogy with ley lines, right? So ley lines are places where the Plane of Magic is sort of closer somehow to the world of Taelgar. There are stories in lore of gods being able to imbue some of their power into places or things that then kind of function like ley lines for divine magic.

DM: So a heart imagery could it be associated with that, right? So like the Heart of Shakun could be something that was imbued with Shakun's power or like you know the, the—this sort of thing is often—and I even in dwarven lore there's you know examples of this, where there's item, or you know particular sacred things that were imbued with usually runic power by the Firstborn, by the—by Bahrazel, that then act as kind of particular foci for divine magic. But you don't know any stories of the Dunmari pantheon specifically. But, But that's what comes to mind.
Kenzo: And do I know any, any.

DM: No, just what I already said about, about like I mean you've heard the same kinds of tales about sacred places in across Dunmar are supposed to be places where prayers are you know more likely to be heard, things like that. But heart imagery specifically, there's nothing.

Kenzo: What about like, like other, other organs of god's like the heart of god or like the brain of a god or you know actually imbued into physical objects in the world, but maybe yeah it's sort of like a storm giant's eyes, I guess it sort of as real do like you know is that—is that a thing?
Kenzo: Like it's Shakun's brain like a rock on the top of a mountain someplace?

DM: Yeah, you haven't—you have not heard anything. There's, there's no stories to this effect, right? There's no, like—it's not so much physical pieces of god's being left behind. It's just places where they can hear you better, right? It's places where there's the sort of divine power collects for, for some reason. And, and many of the meal—many monasteries are, are, are built on those places right, so the Lakan monastery near Tokra is like, you know, an ancient site where, early in Dunmar history, the, the sort of first settlers gathered and it was kind of a point where people would gather to share knowledge and, and stories, and so that kind of developed as a particularly sacred spot to, to Laka. But there's not, um, it's not like the storm giant's at all, at least in your understanding. It's not like there's some physical embodiment of a god. It's something that over time would accumulate the sort of resonance with god.

Kenzo: But then the other thing about like this particular template—to temple as well—Bhishma, Bhishma sacrifice themselves, or what happened at the exact spot where the pet—like that, where the pentagon is like.
DM: Jeevali. So Jeevali was the goddess who cleansed the land, but used up all her power in doing so, and then Bhishma sacrificed herself to bring Jeevali back.
Kenzo: And that all happen like right here at this—
DM: That all happened basically here, yes.
Seeker: Whoa. On the edge of the river that used to run around the bend here.
Seeker: And Jeevali was cleansing the land of what?
DM: The plague. The First Plague, the thing that destroyed Drankor.
Wellby: Where the heart was before it went missing?
Seeker: I don't think we know anything about the heart aside from Kenzo's vision of it.
Kenzo: Well, we know who would have the answer to that. That's right.
Seeker: Lovely. We also—it was something that—the implication was something had been taken or is missing from the monastery at Karawa. From the temple, sorry.

Kenzo: I think, given Candrosa's state before when we left, and their unwillingness to share what had occurred there, I think either the, either the heart was stolen or—who knows? Maybe, maybe, maybe—renewed given away from blackmail or somehow taken.
Seeker: I still think Candrosa was somehow—yeah, under duress, yeah—either guilt—through guilt or shame or some enchantment, or some blackmail, like you said. We don't know.

before: Wellby: I think maybe with the snacks that you pulled out like we've been trading favorite recipes but from back home. Welcome—elven and elven-halfling food is like not, not the food that we make in elven-halfling restaurants to sell to humans, but like—right.
Unknown: The actual—right.
Kenzo: Are there fusion halfling-elf restaurants, and like halflings that make elf food, and like—
Seeker: Maybe there will be now.
Wellby: I've been laying down on the table, relaxing, and I sit up and said, What, what happened?
after: Kenzo: I agree. Is anybody able to heal me?
Seeker: Oh yes, of course. Let me give you an additional word of healing. Just a moment.
DM: I mean, you could stick around for another hour and take a short rest.
Wellby: Go, if we can, before it gets dark, do you think?
Kenzo: Yeah.

interactions.title: Wellby finds and reads a monk’s unfinished diary
lines: DM: Okay, so it's pretty cursory search within each one. Um, the bathhouse is where the orc is tied up. You already kind of looked in there when you left that orc. Um, I don't know if you want to open the doors or not. So, starting in the dormitories—I mean, these are—there are three-story like sandstone buildings. They've both been fairly well looted, presumably in part recently by the orcs, but some of the damage seems to be quite old, so this has probably been looted multiple times. Um, you do find, poking around, a few hundred sort of scattered small silver and copper coins. A total of 24 silver and 160 copper, just like you know little kick—you know, things kicked in the dust, hidden around a little bit. Um, and the other thing you find is a small diary, written in Dunmari.

DM: An unnamed monk who seemed to have lived here perhaps just before the Great War. You sort of flip through it really quickly, and it's sort of describing like life in the monastery. I'm—skipping to the end: growing militarization, attacks, news of distant heroes and great councils. Then no news, which is worse. Then everybody running. And the last entry is, I'm choosing to stay here with the others, contribute what I can to protecting our great work. Bhishma, watch over my soul. And there are no further entries.
Delwath: Recording of all the stories, right, is their—
DM: Is their great work. ((unrelated workshop description))

before: Seeker: Memorialize the dead.
Wellby: Perception, did you say? Yep.
Kenzo: Yeah.
DM: So, um, I use—you spend, I guess, what, most of the hour searching, or do you want to go somewhere else?
Wellby: I'm willing to cover the bathhouse, the dormitories, and those two little buildings.
after: DM: And, ah, except tucked in the corner, you do find an odd piece of vellum that seems to be in unusually good condition. I'm—blank, nothing's written on it that you can see, anyway. But you would not expect it necessarily to have lasted, and sort of tucked away um you know, on a bench. And then anything else you wanted to—what else did you want to search?
Unknown: Um.
Wellby: Let's see, we talked about the two dormitories, the two workshops. I'd love to stick my head down the well, in case it's an extra like escape route in an emergency.

DM: Ah, OK, the well. The one that was sort of back behind the bathhouse? Yeah, um, yeah. It connects—that it, it, it goes down at that—it's dry now, but it looks like it was connected to some sort of underwater—underground cistern water works, so you stick your head down, and you can see—well, you can't really. I guess you could drop your driftglobe down, and then it would bounce back up, because if it's more than 60 feet away from you, it goes to within 60 feet. So there's like a large empty cistern at the bottom of the well, and seems to be connected to a—like a—an inflow tunnel and another outflow tunnel, all dry now. There's—possibly connecting to the bathhouse somehow, although there's no well in the bath house or possibly connecting to the fountain that you saw that's, that's here, that's sort of in the middle.

Wellby: So there's two—those two big like sewer-pipe the kind of things we walk past. The idea that those were probably like below the level of the river, and then the river would have flown in to fill the cistern, yes?

Seeker: So it's a way to like write a really powerful rune on there, and then you can read it off and then have that at a moment's notice. Let's hold on to that, yeah.

after: Kenzo: Turn this to—[garbled].
Seeker: Over us.

Seeker: And the Hall of Stories. And the temple. I think we haven't been into either, right?

interactions.title: The courtyard fountain conjures ordinary water
lines: DM: So the central courtyard here is—it has the spiral labyrinth, a path that twists in a spiral in towards the center, made of crushed stone, sort of decorative. With these stone baths—the stone benches, sorry—on the sides. The fountain itself is still—water is still flowing and seems to, um—although some of the, the stone benches have been, you know, sort of—the orcs have like chipped at them, and there's one that has like graffiti scrawled on it. I'm—the fountain itself seems to be still pure water and not particularly harmed in any way. And there's like—I'm—trickles of water that flow out from the fountain and collecting in small streams that flow towards the benches on the outside of the labyrinth and then collect in these pools. But the water doesn't go anywhere from there, and you can't see any—there's no like waterworks mechanism here. I'm—I'm—
Kenzo: Do the benches say like Grash on them and, like spray paint, or there's, there's—they're like orc like street art isn't like little, little or you know—
DM: Maybe choose—no, it's, it's pretty much like you know Grash will never die, and, you know—
DM: Right, that—it's that kind of graffiti. It's not you know.

DM: It's not orc art, yeah. It's pretty crude. I mean there's like some, though, like you know that—I'm—rising-sun symbol that you saw is painted in a few places, and us the stone path has been sort of kicked up in places in some like rocks have been kicked into these pools on the side. But the fountain itself seems unharmed. The fountain is—it's a sort of abstract sort of curvy design, kind of reminiscent of a, of a human kind of abstractly shaped out of flowing water. And it's—the fountain itself is made of polished petrified wood. And the water is kind of flowing down on—you can sort of almost imagine that it's kind of flowing out like tears, but kind of around the entire sort of just flowing down around the sides of this, of this fountain, and then collecting at the bottom and flowing out of these little rivulets to the, to the pools.
Seeker: Lean in close. I attempted to touch the actual surface of the petrified-wood sculpture. I put my hand through the water.
DM: Feels cool and clean and refreshing. The wood itself is—or the sculpture—is well-crafted. It's smooth and polished. Feels cool to the touch in the hot desert sun.
Seeker: Where would you find petrified wood? Geez I guess that's just something that's like it's almost like a fossil. You dig up somewhere.
Seeker: It is presumably a magical fountain. I know I've got my purple goggles stowed on my forehead, quick access, so I pop them in.
Delwath: I was just gonna—I was gonna concentrate on Fey Sight while everybody's looking at the fountain to the detail. Okay, they got my—
DM: So the fountain is indeed magical. I'm—both Seeker and, and note that.
Unknown: Um, hold on. It is—
Wellby: That's where the water is coming from, then, yeah.
Delwath: Is there—is, is, is the whole thing magic? Is there a source? Is it like the sculpture, or like where does the aura—is it radiating over the whole thing, or is it—
Delwath: How big was a sculpture?
DM: It's nearly the size of it—I mean, it's basically life-size, is like the size of a person, six feet tall, five—
Kenzo: Wait, so it's just a magic fountain that is like making water, the past—it's not like we, we, we bathe ourselves in it and we get hit points back or get magical—
DM: No, it's just magic fountain that's making water.
Seeker: I drank a little bit. It was good.
DM: Yes, exactly. It's a fountain of thirst quenching.

interactions.title: A ghost guardian recognizes Kenzo and admits the party
lines: DM: So, as you pull this ponderous wooden door open, it begins—it begins to swing, swing out. Drifting forward are four ghostly figures. They are—it's hard to see their features because there's—they're robed and hooded, and the hoods are covering, covering their faces. And they're holding their arms kind of in their sleeves a little bit like this. One holding a quarter staff. One—two holding quarterstaffs, the other two unarmed. And as the door swings open, they drift forward and kind of form a phalanx blocking the door. And one holding a staff kind of comes forward and stands on the stairs and puts the staff down in front, and you hear this kind of ghostly sort of faint voice echoing: Turn back. This tower is protected.
DM: I mean, they're, they're ghosts and look—
Kenzo: Are your posture, like I mean because, you know, also you don't remember how like Lakan Mystai have like—yeah. It does, it does. He gives, he gives them the some.

Kenzo: Kenzo, Kenzo like you see Kenzo says that, because the—you know, this is protected. Kenzo like gets down on one knee and kind of does like a swirling motion and then like [garbled]. And then it's just going to sneering incredibly, you know, with—on one knee, like looking—when—my brother. And you know Kenzo stands and looks at him and says, Brother, we've returned.

Kenzo: Seek knowledge. We seek to understand what happened thirty years ago.

Kenzo: We've slain, we've slain the orcs that were here [garbled]. I'm Kenzo. Kenzo of Chardon, of, of the Lakan Mystai in addition. And my companions—

Kenzo: Then, before they do that, I say, Perhaps we can help you remember. We will, we will try to help him—help you remember your name.
Kenzo: Sort of look back at the companions. Well, that works.

interactions.title: The memory of Karmana’s last defense and ghostly duty
lines: DM: Okay, make a, make a Charisma check. So, as, as the—as this old—this monk is kind of droning on a little bit, and the memory of the young initiate-to-be is turning, you know as faded from the speech and as—I'm—turning to you know his worries about what's going to happen next, Delwath kind of reaches out and the scene shifts. And for a minute, you see a battlefield. I'm—dead elves, dead hob goblins scattered across. One elf kind of beginning to push himself up from among the dead, wipe his face. And then the scene shifts, and you are standing outside the monastery.

DM: You are strong. You are fighting what seems like a sea of undead. Skeletons 20, 30 more of them coming for the doors, some blasting with magic, and your companions are falling around you. The, the small group of monks that are sort of guarding the doors—to the dark version here—the small group of monks that are guarding the doors begin to fall. One, two, three. The scallop—the skeleton army parts, and walking down among you know, with 10—the 10–15 skeletons that are surviving is a skeletal creature, but with intelligence in its eyes.

DM: And it holds out a hand, and not just this blast of dark energy shoots out of his hand, and one of your companion monks is just blasted. And you step forward, preparing to fight this thing. Charge at—the battle is intense, and you can feel it strike the killing blow. But there is no way you will let these creatures into the monastery. There is, there is no way. That is not happening today or ever. And as you die, your soul does not leave the world, and you remember the moment of dying, and you remember the moment of the pain. And then—

interactions.title: Karmana explains the Hall’s darkness, his charge, and the failed expedition
lines: DM: So, as the door swings open, you can see that this was a bedroom. There's a simple wooden bed, not particularly ornate, a wardrobe that similarly plain, and a small table with a brass candelabra on it, holding—designed to hold six thin tapers, and an ivory box that has been—that is carved with a rendition of riders on horseback herding flocks of goats. And drifting across the bed, sort of pacing back and forth but moving through the bed each time a paces back and forth, is a ghostly figure who turns to look at you, surprised, as you enter.

DM: He is faint as his features are sort of slightly indistinct, like they've sort of softened with time and age—can not quite fully remember his face. But he is wearing robes of the, of the Mystai of Bhishma and, and you recognize this ghostly figure from the first memory that you encountered in the Hall of Stories, as the one who told the undead army, you will not enter. And turns to look at you as you approach with some surprise. Turning, turning and sort of raising his fists slightly and saying, who are you?
Kenzo: Kenzo does the, does the gesture of the initiates and it gets down on one knee and proceeds to do the ritual greeting. Brother.
DM: Got past my brethren, but who are you to use our signs and symbols?
Kenzo: I'm Kenzo, an initiate of Bhishma. And also an initiate of Laka.
DM: There have been no initiates of Bhishma since I fell defending this tower. How could you be an initiate?
Kenzo: Jeevali asked for my life, and—
DM: He'll start to look closer at you. That is a surprising thing, but I see no lie in you.
DM: What of your companions? Who are they?
Kenzo: Were in fellowship. We all seek understanding of what is unfolding, what happened here 30 years ago, and what we must do now. Do you know of Rai?
DM: I know the name, yes.
Kenzo: You know of the quest and 30 years ago that the order was to undertake in collaboration with Rai?
DM: I remember some, yes. What is your concern with such history?

Kenzo: We believe that whatever happened 30 years ago is deeply connected to the corruption in the land that's unfolding today. Strange demons are found throughout the land. Corruption that concerns the centaurs. Destruction amongst the gods, Shakun now unable to protect Dunmar. We believe all this is connected somehow to what happened 30 years ago, and also potentially Rai's disappearance, or whatever happened to him. Are you aware of any of this news?
DM: There has been a darkness growing in the land, yes. Something changed. Some, some force of protection, something that was keeping the rot from spreading, somehow failed.
Kenzo: The Heart of Shakun. That's what Bhishma told me.
DM: Perhaps, but I—perhaps. This has been growing for many years.

DM: There is a—when most of my order left and did not return, something was freed. Something was—something that had been watching over the land ceased to do so. And every year since then, there have been more things we've had to drive off.
Kenzo: Since when? Since 30 years ago, since 30 years ago—you know what happened? What happened to your order? What were they trying to accomplish, and what happened? What was the outcome?
DM: They were trying to close some portal, and I presume they must have failed.
Kenzo: Where did the undead army come from?
DM: I cannot leave this tower. I don't know where they came from, only that they came here. Even before I died, I stayed behind to protect our stories. And now I cannot leave this tower.
Delwath: What is the darkness in the Hall?

DM: That is a sad story. Sajan. That is her name. She was the, she was the master of the archives many years ago, when the Great War and the plague struck and all who lived here died. She bound herself to the Hall of Stories. She wove a web of snares and nightmares that those who would seek to destroy us, that would seek evil of this place, were caught in. But she is lost. And if you try to find memories that touch upon darkness, sometimes she will rise and take control. Oh, 20 years or so after the plague that we were able to come back, reclaim the monastery. And by that, it was too late. We did not know how to save her.
DM: Maybe someday a new living master will come and figure out a way to heal her. But during my time, we just tried to show her happy memories when we could.
DM: Sorry, hold on one sec.
DM: My name is Karmana, the last master of the Mystai.
Kenzo: Karmana, if you're the last master, can you share more about the nature of—
Kenzo: What should happen now, of what happened, which failed to happen before, that needs to happen now?
DM: I do not know what should or should not happen. That is not my purpose. My purpose is to protect the tower, protect the Hall of Stories.

DM: I know that darkness has grown. I know that just under a year ago, there was a great wave of darkness, foul stench of a rotten ocean that washed across us, coming from Kharsan then. Something is there now. Some, some creature, object of power.

DM: And these dangers have grown. We hold on by a thread. There are—the orcs are growing more numerous every day, and their fear of the ghosts may not last forever. We are strong, but a determined army perhaps could break through. I know that—I don't know how all of these things are connected, but I know that whatever happened 30 years ago, uh, well, caused, allowed, or somehow—that failure let evil into this world.
Kenzo: Where there any survivors that—where's—were there when whatever was unleashed was unleashed? Did anybody see it? Was any—is there any survivor from that time?
DM: None return from the east to this monastery.
DM: She left before they left, before they turned east. Most went east. A few stayed with me to protect the monastery. And it Saka turned west.
Kenzo: Is there any more questions for last master of Bhishma, who was not there at the moment that we needed somebody to be there to witness whatever the fuck we don't understand?
Wellby: What he's gonna say—that's true. [garbled] We send our gratitude or welcome in conversation. What's it like being a ghost?
DM: It is, it is different. It is hard to think of things that are not—that are not defending the tower, defending the Hall. It is hard to force my mind to remember the past. My purpose is all now.
Wellby: Do you feel days passing?
DM: I feel moments in time.
Kenzo: You know who the skeletons are downstairs?

DM: Some are my companions who died fighting. Some perhaps our orcs or hobgoblins or other creatures that wandered into Sajan's traps and were ensnared and died of hunger, thirst, wandering and despairing memories of the dark.
Wellby: That's true. Do you have unfinished business outside this tower that we can bring to rest for you?
DM: If I once did, I can no longer remember it. All that consumes my mind is seeing this monastery's safe.
Seeker: What's in your beautiful ivory box?
DM: You may take that. Possessions mean nothing to me anymore.
Seeker: I pick it up to look at it.

DM: It's—ah, it has—it holds the candles for the candelabra. There's six of them. It's a decent—it's not a—I mean, it's a pretty nicely carved box. It's, you know, it has the scene of riders on horseback herding a flock of goats. It's a very sort of pastoral. It's intricately done.
Wellby: Didn't he just give it to you?
DM: Say you could take it. Possessions mean nothing to me.
Kenzo: The one time we're actually given permission, it's now official yet.
Wellby: We did—by—know—I respect the way that Seeker each birthday would refuse to accept presents because they were looted.
Kenzo: You know where the heart of—
DM: That is not my—as I said to your friend, it is difficult to focus on anything that is not my purpose.
Seeker: Have you seen visitors from Chardon? Has anyone from the Society of the Open Scroll been here and tried to enter?

DM: No. There was recently, though, some odd creatures that pass through, some of which got eaten by the flying beast that lives outside. They were, they were almost like human-hyena creatures that they seem nearly undead themselves.
DM: But no humans have been in my tower, anyway, until you.
Seeker: Have you ever met a small, purple, winged, sarcastic lizard?
DM: I have heard tales of this creature. I have not made the journey, so I have not met that creature, no.
Kenzo: You know the nature of the danger 30 years ago, and is it the same danger we faced now?

DM: I can only say the danger I perceive to my realm. But I will say this: when I was alive 40 years ago, this place felt—not safe. Kharsan is full of ghosts and the haunted dead, and always has been since the plague. But it didn't feel in imminent danger. And then the monks left, my friends, with Rai, never came back. And whether it was their failure, whether they open something that should have been closed, whether it was simply that the power of the monks—and I mean, we were not a helpless order. Many of us traveled across the land, helping those who needed help and giving protection, and, and if you've heard any stories of Rai, you know that he was far from power less—whether it was—
Delwath: That they open something that—

DM: Should have been closed, or attracted the attention of something that should have been left unwatched, or whether it was simply that those who protected the land failed and their protection vanished. Since that event 30 years ago, darkness has crept back into the shadows. And I can feel the danger closing in around this tower. Cannot tell you who or what might be in danger outside my domain.
Seeker: Did you say the monks left from here with Rai?

DM: Bay—they—no, Rai was never here. They left—I guess Rai was supposed to meet them, or I don't, I don't know the details of their exact plan. There was some discussion among those who were leaving just before they left, and those of us who stayed we're preparing for our own journeys.
Kenzo: You know why Rai needed your help?

DM: I was never one who was— He seems like he's sort of struggling with his memories a little bit, um. It is hard for me to remember what happened before if it does not concern the defense of this tower. My order has long been concerned with not just memories and stories, but the echoes and resonances of those stories elsewhere, among the planes of souls. I presume Rai's mastery is in other parts of magic, and perhaps needed help connecting somehow—
DM: Whether to the gods or the energy of the Plane of Consciousness, or something else I cannot imagine, I would not speculate. And I fear those details are drifting from my mind.
DM: But whatever happened, the danger has grown year by year, until last year, when something changed again and the darkness coalesced at Kharsan. This creature Grash the orcs talk of.
Wellby: You see them building his temple from your tower?

DM: Cannot see from my tower, no. I hear sometimes them talking below. They will not linger too far—too near the tower, for the ghosts scare them, but sound carries in the night desert air, and sometimes they will sit and talk outside their base. And if they say things that concern the defense of my domain, my hearing is heightened.
Wellby: Is this the top floor of the towers that we're building?
DM: This is the top floor.
